                          SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS OF
                         THE MISO TRANSMISSION OWNERS

          The MISO Transmission Owners1 submit these supplemental comments in

response to the Notice Inviting Comments issued by the Federal Energy Regulatory

Commission (“Commission”) in the above-captioned docket on October 27, 2025,

regarding the Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking released by the Secretary of Energy

(“Secretary”) on October 23, 2025.2 The MISO Transmission Owners are submitting these

       As stated in our prior comments,3 the MISO Transmission Owners strongly support

the ANOPR’s goals of interconnecting large loads in a timely and reliable manner that

avoids unfair cost shifts. The MISO Transmission Owners have long been committed to

ensuring a robust transmission system and facilitating and maintaining resource adequacy

in the region. The MISO Transmission Owners, like the current Administration, are

acutely aware that both transmission and generation are vital to ensuring resiliency,

reliability, and affordability and have worked to advance the development of both to

support load integration.4 Although this long-term commitment has positioned the MISO

region to support new large loads, the MISO Transmission Owners acknowledge that more

can, and should, be done to ensure that the MISO region can speed up large load integration

leadership.5 To that end, the MISO Transmission Owners provide this update on our

continuing efforts, and progress, to improve the speed to power for large loads.

       Since filing our earlier comments in this proceeding, the MISO Transmission

Owners have continued working to facilitate the interconnection of large loads in the MISO

region. As discussed in more detail below, the MISO Transmission Owners continue to

utilize MISO’s open, transparent, and streamlined Expedited Project Review (“EPR”)

process to review and approve urgent transmission projects to serve load, including large

loads, fastest than the regular MISO Transmission Expansion Plan (“MTEP”) cycle. In

addition, the MISO Transmission Owners are active participants in several MISO

stakeholder initiatives specifically designed to improve speed to power for large loads

while ensuring reliability, including consideration of a new Zero-Injection Generator

Interconnection Agreement (“ZGIA”) and new reliability requirements regarding large

loads, both of which are discussed below.

       Bear in mind that these efforts are not the whole picture. As highlighted by the

Edison Electric Institute (“EEI”) in its recent comments6 to the Commission and the

comments of the Entergy Operating Companies,7 various stakeholders in the MISO region

continue to work together to integrate loads timely and reliably without other customers

MISO Transmission Owners and MISO explained in previous comments,13 the MISO

in managing and interconnecting loads, including large loads, and these Supplemental

       The MISO Transmission Owners urge the Commission to keep this evidence top

regions are the same when it comes to interconnecting large loads. As the Commission

itself has highlighted, “unlike Eastern [Regional Transmission Organizations (“RTOs”)],

restructured retail markets,” a composition which “enables LSEs and regulators in the

region to undertake longer-term commitments to generation resources, either in the form

of direct construction by incumbent LSEs or through comparable long-term contracts.”14

This composition, where states play the primary role in resource adequacy, has long been

       To be clear, the MISO Transmission Owners welcome any and all support from the

Commission that avoids a “one-size-fits-all” approach and provides flexibility and

encourages Federal Power Act section 205 filings to craft innovative solutions that

optimize regional differences in achieving timely, reliable, and affordable speed to power.

Doing so will ensure that the region’s finite time and resources are used to focus on

solutions that efficiently, reliably, and fairly integrate new large load in the region.

I.     SPEED TO POWER

       Since filing our earlier comments in this proceeding, the MISO Transmission

Owners have continued working at the state and federal levels to ensure that speed to power

is more than an aspirational slogan.20 The MISO Transmission Owners recognize that

more can be done in pursuit of accelerating speed to power and as described below, the

MISO Transmission Owners continue to make use of every tool in the existing toolbox, as

well consider additional reforms and participate in various MISO-stakeholder initiatives

specifically geared to identifying new tools for integrating load timely and reliably.

        A.      Transmission

       In pursuing additional reforms to accelerate speed to power, it is important to

evaluate tools that would speed up transmission development for large load integration, as

large load timelines are often driven by economic development, national security, and

technological imperatives. Creating streamlined processes and ensuring the ability of

transmission owners to act expeditiously are just a few examples of the tools that are critical

to achieving the ANOPR’s objectives.

               1.      Proactive Long Range Transmission Planning

       It is no secret that the sooner long range, backbone transmission is built the faster

generation and load can come online.          Transmission serves as the critical conduit

connecting load with generation. Regional transmission, in particular, is key to supporting

interstate energy transfers, providing economic value through least-cost energy

procurement, bolstering regional reliability, and supporting the integration of generation

and load. Since its inception, MISO and its members have recognized and worked to

realize these benefits.21 Since 2003, MISO’s MTEP has “guided the approval of more than

6,800 total projects and upgraded or added nearly 79,000 miles of transmission

infrastructure, with over 10,000 miles of transmission line additions or improvements

planned.”22    In fact, the Commission has specifically recognized MISO’s regional

        B.        Generation

                 1.    ERAS

       The Expedited Resource Addition Study (“ERAS”) process, which was approved

by the Commission in July 2025, is designed to fast-track needed new generation to meet

growing load. On March 9, 2026, MISO announced the third cycle of projects to be

evaluated under the ERAS process.31      This cycle includes fifteen projects totaling

approximately 8 GW of proposed new capacity and features a mix of natural gas resources

and battery storage spread across MISO’s North, Central, and South regions. MISO states

that all projects are expected to be in service by 2031 or earlier. Since the program

launched, “53 projects representing nearly 27 GW of proposed capacity have been accepted

or are pending validation into ERAS” and “[t]en have already advanced to completed

generator interconnection agreements [(“GIAs”)], with an additional 15 projects nearing

completion.”32

                 2.    JTIQ

       The MISO Transmission Owners supported the filing by MISO, together with

Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”), to implement the Joint Targeted Interconnection

Queue (“JTIQ”) framework, which enables MISO and SPP to develop a portfolio of

backbone network upgrades to facilitate the interconnection of over 28 GW of generation

                1.      Defining “Large Load” and Related Interconnection Reliability
                       Requirements.

       Because large loads can have a disproportionate impact on system reliability due to

their size and unique characteristics, MISO is pursuing the development of reliability

requirements related to the integration of large loads, including defining a “large load.”

Consistent with our Initial Comments regarding the Second Principle of the ANOPR, the

MISO Transmission Owners generally support a definition that avoids a threshold based

solely on the MW size of the load and instead provides reasonable flexibility in defining

large loads, given the technical experience and judgment that is required to appropriately

and reasonably weigh operational, reliability, and administrative factors that are critical to

defining large loads. Currently, MISO expects to file Tariff revisions including such new

requirements in June 2026.35

               2.      ZGIA

       MISO is discussing with stakeholders its proposal for a ZGIA for generation co-

located with load. The Third Principle of the ANOPR recognized that siting a large load

near or at the same point of interconnection as a new generating facility could reduce the

network upgrades needed to interconnect only the load or only the generating facility.

MISO’s proposed ZGIA is specifically designed with that goal in mind. The ZGIA would

allow a generator to serve load directly but grants no interconnection service. The proposed

ZGIA process leverages existing interconnection frameworks in terms of study aspects,
